motion: Does the God of the Bible exist?

bridges.description: Positive reasons offered for the existence of the biblical God.
Observed functional complexity is traced to an intelligent designer identified with the biblical God.
Objective moral duties are traced to a standard grounded in God's nature.
Biblical coherence, prophecy, and the resurrection identify the designer and moral ground as the biblical God.
Reasons offered for concluding that the biblical God does not exist.
Mutually incompatible attributed properties are presented as ruling out the biblical God's existence.
Natural accounts of complexity and morality are offered in place of divine explanation.
Challenges to biblical reliability and Christian historical claims undercut identification of a real biblical God.

sections.title: Existence claim and definition
sections.rationale: The debate distinguishes general probability from the claimed certainty of the biblical-God question and tests whether the proposed nonmaterial being is coherently defined.

sections.title: Design and natural explanation
sections.rationale: Butt's positive design inference and Barker's naturalistic objection form a central exchange about whether observed complexity supports a designer.

sections.title: Morality and human value
sections.rationale: The speakers contest objective moral grounding, natural altruism, and distinctive human value.

sections.title: Biblical coherence and reliability
sections.rationale: Alleged contradictions, contextual answers, interpretation, and scriptural reliability directly affect the specifically biblical identification.

sections.title: Divine agency and character
sections.rationale: Foreknowledge, created agency, hell, and the moral standard attributed to God test the coherence and character of the proposed deity.

sections.title: History and salvation claims
sections.rationale: Falsifiability, Jesus, resurrection, and salvation claims connect the biblical-God case to asserted history.

sections.title: Situational moral cases
sections.rationale: The cross-examination tests harm-minimization through an extreme forced choice, a Nazi-doctor example, Barker's shared-law answer, and Butt's consistency follow-up.
